tasks.q: Press Run and read both lines it displays.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
Look at the sign in the middle of each comparison.
tasks.fb: A comparison does not need an if. On its own it already gives you True or False.
tasks.starter:
print(7 > 3)
print(7 < 3)

teach.say: A comparison asks a question about two values. The answer is always one of two words: True or False. Python works the comparison out and hands that word back, so print() can display it.

lines: Ask whether 7 is greater than 3, which it is.
Ask whether 7 is less than 3, which it is not.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: == asks a question and gives True or False. A single = stores a value and gives nothing back.

teach.say: == asks whether two values are the same. One = would store a value instead, so the two signs do completely different jobs.

tasks.q: Change the sign in the middle so the program displays True.
brief: Change only the sign between a and b.
Do not change either number.
Display exactly: True
tasks.fb: == and != are opposites. Whenever one is True the other is False.
tasks.starter:
a = 4
b = 9
print(a == b)

tests.why: False came out, so the program is still asking whether the two are the same. 4 and 9 are not the same, so ask about being different instead.

hint.think: `4` and `9` are not the same. Which sign asks about being different?
walk: == asks whether two values are the same.
There is a second sign that asks the opposite.
It is the one you met in the worked example above.

teach.say: != asks whether two values are different. It is True exactly when == would be False.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: Two equal values are not less than each other, but they are less than or equal. A value that is only ever True or False is called a boolean.

teach.say: < is True only when the left value is the smaller one. <= is also True when the two are equal, and that one extra case is the whole difference between them.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it displays True, because a mark of exactly `40` is a pass.
brief: Line 1 is written for you.
Replace ____ with one comparison sign.
A mark of `40` counts as a pass, so `40` itself must give True.
Display exactly: True
tasks.fb: The pass mark itself has to count as a pass, so `40` or more means >= `40`, never > `40`.
tasks.starter:
mark = 40
print(mark ____ 40)

tests.why: Replace the ____ with one sign. If False came out, the sign you chose does not allow the two values to be equal.

hint.think: You need a sign that is True for bigger and also True for equal.
walk: > is True for bigger but not for equal.
== is True for equal but not for bigger.
One sign does both jobs at once.

teach.say: >= is True when the left value is the bigger one and also when the two are equal.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display True when it is greater than `10`. Display False when it is not.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
The `10` is written into your program, not typed in.
One line of output, which is True or False.
tasks.fb: No if is needed. The comparison is already True or False, so print() can display it straight out.
tasks.starter: # Read one number and display the comparison

tests.why: 25 is greater than 10, so the comparison is True.
4 is not greater than 10. True here means the comparison was written the wrong way round.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. Exactly 10 is not greater than 10, so > gives False and >= would wrongly give True.

hint.think: Read the number, then display the comparison itself.

teach.say: A comparison can use a variable on one side and a fixed number on the other.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a second word. Display True when the two words are the same. Display False when they are not.
brief: The user types in two lines, one word on each.
Every letter has to match, so a different spelling is a different word.
One line of output, which is True or False.
tasks.fb: == compares words as well as numbers, and the match has to be exact, letter for letter.
tasks.starter: # Read two words and display whether they match

tests.why: The same word twice, so == is True.
Two different words. True here means the two words were never actually compared.
One extra letter makes a different word, so == is False.

hint.think: Words are compared with the same sign as numbers.

tasks.q: This program should display True when the number typed is greater than `10`. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and read the error message.
The user types in one whole number.
One line of output, which is True or False.
tasks.fb: Casting comes back in every lesson. A value typed in is text until int() turns it into a number.
tasks.starter:
n = input()
print(n > 10)

tests.why: A TypeError here means text was compared with a number. Put the input() inside int( ).
Cast on the way in, then the comparison works for any number.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. Once the cast is right, exactly 10 is not greater than 10.

hint.think: Read the error. input() always hands back text, and text cannot be compared with a number.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display whether it is below `0`. Then display whether it is exactly `0` on the next line. Then display whether it is above `0` on the next line.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
Three lines of output, each one True or False.
Exactly one of the three lines is True.
The `0` is written into your program, not typed in.
tasks.fb: Three comparisons on one value divide every possible number into three groups with no overlap.
tasks.starter: # One number, three comparisons, three lines

tests.why: A negative number is below 0 and nothing else.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. 0 is neither below nor above 0, so only the middle line is True.
A positive number is above 0 and nothing else.
Just one below the boundary, and still only the first line is True.

hint.think: Three comparisons on the same variable, each one displayed on its own line.
walk: Read the number and cast it.
Display the comparison for below.
Display the comparison for exactly.
Display the comparison for above.

tasks.q: Press Run. Then count the spaces at the start of each line.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
Line 3 starts four spaces in. Line 4 does not.
Change the 8 to a 2 and Run again to see which line disappears.
tasks.fb: The colon opens the if and the four spaces say what is inside it. Python needs both.
tasks.starter:
n = 8
if n > 5:
    print("big")
print("done")

teach.say: An if asks a question and only runs some lines when the answer is True. Two things say which lines those are. The if line ends with a colon, and the lines inside it are indented four spaces.

lines: Remember the number 8 under the name n.
Ask whether n is greater than 5. The colon at the end says lines follow.
This line is indented four spaces, so it only runs when the answer is True.
This line is not indented, so it runs every time.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: 2 is not greater than 5, so the indented line is skipped. The line that is not indented runs whatever the answer was.

teach.say: The indent is not decoration. Python reads it to decide which lines belong to the if and which lines come after it and always run.

tasks.q: Change the program so a number of exactly `100` is counted as `"full"`.
brief: Change only the comparison sign.
Do not change either number.
Display exactly: full
tasks.fb: This is the boundary mistake, and it is the commonest one in this lesson. Ask yourself every time whether the edge value itself should count.

tests.why: Nothing was displayed, so the question was False. 100 is not greater than 100, so > has to become the sign that also allows equal.

hint.think: `100` has to count, so the sign must allow the two values to be equal.
walk: Nothing is displayed, so the question came out False.
`100` is not greater than `100`.
There is one sign that is True for greater and for equal.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it displays `"child"` when the age is under `18`.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
Replace ____ with one line.
An age of exactly `18` displays `"adult"`.
Display exactly one word: adult or child
tasks.fb: An if and an else are two branches of one decision. Exactly one of them runs, never both.
tasks.starter:
n = int(input())
if n >= 18:
    print("adult")
____
    print("child")

tests.why: Replace the ____ with the line that opens the other branch. It ends with a colon.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. 18 or more includes 18 itself, so an adult it is.
Below the boundary, so the second branch is the one that runs.

hint.think: One line is missing between the two branches, and it ends with a colon.
walk: The if covers the ages of `18` and over.
One line opens the branch for everything else.
It is not indented, and it ends with a colon.

teach.say: else catches every case the if did not. It has a colon of its own, it is not indented, and the lines inside it are.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number of marks. Display `"pass"` when it is `40` or more. Display `"fail"` when it is less.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
The `40` is written into your program, not typed in.
Display exactly one word: pass or fail
tasks.fb: `40` or more means >= `40`. The exact boundary is always the value worth testing yourself on.
tasks.starter: # Read the marks and display pass or fail

tests.why: Well past the pass mark, so the if branch runs.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. 40 or more includes 40, so fail here means > was used instead of >= .
One below the boundary, so the else branch runs.
A 0 is a number like any other and belongs in the else.

hint.think: One decision with two branches, and the pass mark itself counts as a pass.

teach.say: Mind the boundary. 7 or more means >= 7, so 7 itself counts.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Display `"match"` when the word is `"amber"`. Display `"no match"` when it is not.
brief: The user types in one word.
The word `"amber"` is written into your program.
Display exactly one of: match or no match
tasks.fb: Comparing a word needs the fixed word in quotation marks and the variable without them.
tasks.starter: # Read the word and display match or no match

tests.why: The word is the one being looked for, so the if branch runs.
A different word, so the else runs. match here means the comparison is always True.
Part of the word is not the word. match here means only the first letters were compared.

hint.think: Compare the variable with the fixed word, then choose a branch.

teach.say: An if can compare words with == . The word you are looking for goes in quotation marks, and the variable does not.

tasks.q: This program should display `"big"` or `"small"`. One piece of punctuation is missing. Find it and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and read the error message.
The user types in one whole number.
Do not change either comparison or either word.
Display exactly one word: big or small
tasks.fb: A missing colon stops the program before it starts. The error points at the line after it, so look one line up.
tasks.starter:
n = int(input())
if n > 10
    print("big")
else:
    print("small")

tests.why: A SyntaxError means Python could not read the line. The if line needs a colon at the end, like the else line has.
Once the colon is there the else branch runs for a small number.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. Exactly 10 is not greater than 10, so small is right.

hint.think: Look at the end of the if line and compare it with the end of the else line.
walk: The else line finishes with a mark of punctuation.
Every line that opens a block finishes with the same one.
One line in this program does not.

teach.say: An if line always finishes with a colon. Without it Python stops before the program runs at all and says invalid syntax.

tasks.q: This program should display `"checked"` every time, and `"positive"` as well when the number is above `0`. One line is indented when it should not be. Find it and put it right.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
The word `"checked"` is displayed every single time.
The word `"positive"` is displayed only when the number is above `0`.
Do not change either word.
tasks.fb: Indentation is the whole story here. Python decides what is inside the if by counting the spaces, and nothing else.
tasks.starter:
n = int(input())
if n > 0:
    print("positive")
    print("checked")

tests.why: A positive number displays both lines, and positive comes first.
Nothing came out at all, because both lines are indented inside the if. Only one of them belongs there.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. 0 is not above 0, so only checked is displayed.

hint.think: Which of the two displayed lines should happen whatever the number is?
walk: A line indented four spaces is inside the if.
A line with no spaces in front of it is outside the if.
One of these two lines is in the wrong place.

teach.say: Taking four spaces off the front of a line moves it out of the if, so it runs whatever the answer was.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Then ask for a second whole number. Work out which of them is the larger. Display that number and nothing else.
brief: The user types in two lines, one whole number on each.
When the two are equal, display that value.
One line of output, which is one of the two numbers.
tasks.fb: An if does not have to display words. Either branch can display a value, which is how a program picks one of two.
tasks.starter: # Read two numbers and display the larger one

tests.why: The larger one is the first here, so the if branch displays it.
The larger one is the second here. A program that always displays the first passes only half the tests.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. Two equal values give the same answer either way, so neither branch can be wrong.
With negative numbers the larger one is the one nearer to 0.

hint.think: Compare the two, then display whichever one the comparison points at.
start: # now compare them and display one of them

teach.say: Either branch of an if can display a variable instead of fixed text. That is how a program chooses between two values.

tasks.q: Press Run. Then change the 0 to a 5, Run again, and change it to -5 and Run again.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
Exactly one of the three words is displayed each time.
elif is short for else if.
tasks.fb: One decision, three possible answers, and only ever one of them displayed.

teach.say: elif adds a further question to a decision. It is only asked when every if and elif above it was False. The else at the end catches everything left over.

lines: Remember the number 0 under the name n.
Ask whether n is above 0. It is not, so the next question is asked.
This line is skipped.
Ask whether n is below 0. It is not either.
This line is skipped too.
Nothing was True, so the else runs.
This is the line that is displayed.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: 75 is 70 or more, but it reached the 50 test first and stopped there. Bands have to be written in order, or the wide one swallows the narrow one.

teach.say: Python stops at the first question that is True and skips the rest of the chain, so the order the questions are written in changes the answer.

tasks.q: Change the program so a mark of exactly `50` displays `"pass"`.
brief: Change only one comparison sign.
Do not change any number or any word.
Display exactly: pass
tasks.fb: Every band in a chain has a boundary, and every boundary has to be checked for whether the edge value belongs in or out.

tests.why: fail came out, so the middle question was False. 50 is not greater than 50, so > has to become the sign that also allows equal.

hint.think: `50` has to count as a pass, so the sign in the middle branch must allow equal.
walk: `"fail"` came out, so the middle question was False.
`50` is not greater than `50`.
Only the middle branch needs changing.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it displays `"high"`, `"middle"` or `"low"`.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
Replace ____ with one word.
A number of exactly `50` displays `"low"`.
Display exactly one word: high, middle or low
tasks.fb: elif means ask this only if everything above was False. That is why exactly one branch ever runs.
tasks.starter:
n = int(input())
if n > 100:
    print("high")
____ n > 50:
    print("middle")
else:
    print("low")

tests.why: Replace the ____ with the word that asks a further question. It is short for else if.
The first question was False, so the second one is asked.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. 50 is not more than 50, so nothing matches and the else runs.
Just one past 100, so the first question is True and the rest of the chain is skipped.

hint.think: A second question is being asked, but only when the first one was False.
walk: The word you need is short for else if.
You met it in the Try it at the start of this station.
The rest of the line is already written for you.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display `"positive"` when it is above `0`. Display `"negative"` when it is below `0`. Display `"zero"` when it is exactly `0`.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
One line of output only.
Display exactly one word: positive, negative or zero
tasks.fb: Two questions and an else divide every number into three groups, and `0` is the one most often forgotten.
tasks.starter: # Read the number and describe it in one word

tests.why: Above 0, so the first branch runs.
Below 0. positive here means the number was never compared with 0.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. 0 belongs to neither > 0 nor < 0, which is why the else is needed.
A large negative value still displays one word only, so the branches must not run one after another.

hint.think: Three answers need an if, an elif and an else.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display `"small"` when it is `10` or less. Display `"medium"` when it is more than `10` but `100` or less. Display `"large"` when it is more than `100`.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
Write the bands in order, smallest first.
One line of output only.
Display exactly one word: small, medium or large
tasks.fb: Order the bands from the smallest upwards and each elif only needs one comparison, not two.
tasks.starter: # Read the number and display its band

tests.why: Comfortably inside the lowest band.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. 10 or less includes 10 itself.
One past 10 moves it up a band. small here means the first test is too generous.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. large here means < 100 was used where <= 100 was wanted.
Past every band, so nothing matches and the else runs.

hint.think: Start with the lowest band. Anything that is not in it has already passed `10`.

teach.say: Each elif only needs the top of its own band, because every smaller value was already caught by a branch above it.

tasks.q: This program should display one word only, but a large number makes it display two. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first, then type 250 and look at the output.
The user types in one whole number.
One line of output only.
Change one word, and nothing else.
tasks.fb: Changing the second if into an elif joins the two questions into one decision, and one decision gives one answer.

tests.why: Two words came out. The second if is a new decision, so it is asked even when the first one was True.
Just past 100, and still only one word belongs here.
Only the second question is True, so one word is right either way.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. 50 is not more than 50, so the else runs.

hint.think: The second question is being asked even when the first was already True.
walk: Two separate if statements are two separate decisions.
One chain of questions is a single decision.
One word joins the second question onto the first.

teach.say: Two separate if statements are two separate decisions, so both can run. One chain of if and elif is a single decision, so only one branch can run.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Display `1` when the word is `"red"`. Display `2` when it is `"amber"`. Display `3` when it is `"green"`. Display `0` for any other word.
brief: The user types in one word.
The three words are written into your program.
Display the number only, with no other text.
tasks.fb: A chain of word comparisons is how a program turns a menu choice into an action.
tasks.starter: # Read the word and display its number

tests.why: The second word in the chain, so the question above it was asked first and was False.
The first word in the chain. A 0 here means the word was never compared.
The last of the three named words, so two questions are asked before it.
A word that matches none of the three falls through to the else.

hint.think: Each branch compares the variable with a different fixed word.

teach.say: A chain can compare a word at every step, and the else at the end is what makes an unexpected word safe.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number of marks. Display A when it is `70` or more. Display B when it is `50` or more. Display C when it is `30` or more. Display D for anything less.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
Check the rules in the order they are given.
Write the bands in order, largest first.
Display exactly one letter: A, B, C or D
tasks.fb: An earlier branch wins even when a later one would also be True, so the order of the chain is part of the answer.
tasks.starter: # Read the marks and display one letter

tests.why: Past 50 but not 70, so the second rule is the first one that matches.
Past 70, so the chain stops at the very first question.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. 70 or more includes 70, so B here means > was used instead of >= .
This test sits exactly on the boundary. Exactly 30 is 30 or more, so it is a C and not a D.
Below every band, so nothing matches and the else runs.

hint.think: Written from the largest downwards, each test only needs its own lower edge.
walk: Read the marks and cast them.
Ask about the highest band first.
Add an elif for each band below it.
Finish with an else for everything left.

tasks.q: Press Run. Each line joins two comparisons with the word and.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
Each side of the word and is a complete comparison of its own.
In OCR exam papers these words are written in capitals as AND, OR and NOT.
tasks.fb: and is strict. One False side is enough to make the whole thing False.
tasks.starter:
a = 5
b = 2
print(a > 0 and b > 0)
print(a > 0 and b > 9)

teach.say: and joins two comparisons into one. The whole thing is True only when both sides are True. Each side still needs its own full comparison, with a value on each end.

lines: Remember 5 under the name a.
Remember 2 under the name b.
Both sides are True, so and gives True.
The right-hand side is False, so and gives False.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: or needs only one True side. On the second line neither side is True, so the whole thing is False.

teach.say: or is True when at least one of its two sides is True. Each side still needs a complete comparison, so n == 3 or n == 4 and never n == 3 or 4.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: not flips the answer over. The word was not stop, so the plain comparison is False and the not version is True.

teach.say: not turns True into False and False into True. It goes in front of a comparison and gives you its opposite.

tasks.q: Change the program so both numbers have to be above `3`.
brief: Change only one word.
Do not change any number or any message.
b is exactly `3`, and `3` is not above `3`.
Display exactly: not both
tasks.fb: and and or are a single word apart and give opposite answers most of the time, so read the task carefully before choosing.

tests.why: both big came out, because or is satisfied by one True side. b sits exactly on the boundary: 3 is not above 3, so its side is False. Swap the or for the word that insists on both sides.

hint.think: At the moment one True side is enough. You want to insist on two.
walk: or is happy with one True side.
There is a second joining word that is not.
Only that one word changes.

tasks.q: Finish the program so a rider is `"allowed"` only when they are `12` or older and `140` or taller.
brief: The user types in two lines: an age, then a height in centimetres.
Replace ____ with one word.
An age of exactly `12` and a height of exactly `140` are both allowed.
Display exactly one of: allowed or not allowed
tasks.fb: and is the word for two rules that both have to hold. Each side keeps its own full comparison.

tests.why: Both conditions hold, so the word you need is the strict one.
This test sits exactly on the boundary. 12 or older includes 12 itself, and 140 or taller includes 140 itself, so a rider on both edges is still allowed.
Tall enough but a year too young, and both have to hold.
Old enough but one centimetre short, so the answer is still no.

hint.think: Both conditions have to hold at the same time.
walk: Two rules are given, and neither one may be broken.
One joining word insists on both sides being True.
The two comparisons are already written for you.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display `"special"` when it is `3` or when it is `7`. Display `"ordinary"` when it is neither.
brief: The user types in one whole number.
The `3` and the `7` are written into your program.
Write a full comparison on each side of the or.
Display exactly one word: special or ordinary
tasks.fb: Both sides of an or need a full comparison. n == `3` or `7` is a trap, because it is True whatever n holds.
tasks.starter: # Read the number and decide whether it is one of the two

tests.why: The first allowed value, so the left side of the or is True.
The second allowed value must work too. ordinary here means the or checked only one of them.
Neither value matches. special here usually means it was written n == 3 or 7, which Python treats as True for every number.
A 0 matches neither value, so the else runs.

hint.think: Two values are acceptable, and either one of them is enough.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Display `"allowed"` when the word is not `"locked"`. Display `"blocked"` when it is.
brief: The user types in one word.
The word `"locked"` is written into your program.
Use the word not in your comparison.
Display exactly one word: allowed or blocked
tasks.fb: not turns a comparison into its opposite, which is often easier to read than writing the test the other way round.
tasks.starter: # Read the word and display allowed or blocked

tests.why: Not the word locked, so not flips the False into True.
This is the one word that is blocked. allowed here means the not is missing.
A longer word is not the word locked, so it is still allowed.

hint.think: Write the plain comparison first, then put not in front of it.

tasks.q: This program should display `"special"` for `3` and for `7` only, but it says special for every number. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first, then type 5 and look at the output.
The user types in one whole number.
Do not change either number.
Display exactly one word: special or ordinary
tasks.fb: This is the hardest mistake in the lesson to spot, because Python gives no error at all. It just always says yes.

tests.why: This one was already right, because the left side of the or is True.
Still right, but for the wrong reason: it is the bare 7 making it True, not a comparison.
special came out. The bare 7 on the right of the or is True on its own, so the whole thing is always True.
The right-hand side needs its own full comparison with n.

hint.think: Read the right-hand side of the or on its own. Is it asking a question?

teach.say: Each side of an or has to be a comparison in its own right. A bare number on one side is not a question, and Python treats any number other than 0 as True.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Then ask for a word. Display `"open"` when the number is `3` or `7` and the word is not `"locked"`. Display `"refused"` for anything else.
brief: The user types in two lines: a whole number, then a word.
Put brackets round the or so the and cannot split it.
Display exactly one word: open or refused
tasks.fb: and is worked out before or. An or that has to be judged as one thing needs brackets round it.
tasks.starter: # Read the number and the word, then decide

tests.why: An allowed number with a word that is not locked.
The other allowed number must work too. refused here means the or checked only one of them.
Not an allowed number. open here usually means the or was written n == 3 or 7, which is always True.
The number is allowed but the word is locked, and not turns that into a refusal.

This is the test the brackets are for. open came out because the and grabbed only the 7. Without brackets Python reads the line as n == 3 or (n == 7 and the word test), so a 3 gets through whatever the word says.
Both rules fail, so nothing can let this one through.

hint.think: Two rules both have to hold. The first rule is itself a choice between two numbers.
walk: Read the number and the word.
Write the or for the two allowed numbers.
Put brackets round it.
Join it to the not comparison with and.

tasks.q: Press Run. Then change the word `"check"` to anything else and Run again.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
Count the spaces: the inner if is four in, and its lines are eight in.
With any other word the number is never looked at.
tasks.fb: The outer question decides whether the inner question is asked at all.

teach.say: An if can go inside another if. The inner one is only reached when the outer one was True. Everything inside the inner if is indented a second time, so eight spaces instead of four.

info.title: One = or two
info.text: A single = stores a value and == compares two. Mixing them up is one of the first bugs every programmer meets.

info.title: No switch here
info.text: Some languages have a switch statement for choosing between many options. Python does the same job with elif.

info.title: Unreachable code
info.text: If a band that catches everything is tested first, no branch below it can ever run - those lines are unreachable.

info.title: Same as the gates
info.text: and, or and not behave exactly like the AND, OR and NOT gates you draw truth tables for in topic 2.4.

info.title: Flatten it
info.text: A nested if can often be replaced by one condition joined with and, which is easier to read and easier to test.

info.title: Read the wording
info.text: 'At least', 'no more than' and 'over' all mean different things. Write the boundary value down before you code it.
